source: Gott, Kane, Lesgold (1995) Tutoring for transfer of technical competence (Sherlock 2 evaluation)
finding: Controlled field test of Sherlock 2, a coached-practice troubleshooting tutor for F-15 avionics test stations. Tutored novices matched master technicians on the trained equipment and beat untutored novices.
numbers: 54 airmen: 41 apprentices (18 tutored, 23 untutored; mean 33 months on job), 13 masters (mean 124 months), 3 bases. Groups matched at pretest. Posttest verbal troubleshooting test (VTT): VTT3 control 59 vs tutored 95 vs masters 85 (t=-4.04); VTT4 58 vs 91 vs 86 (t=-3.72); NIT 75 vs 87 vs 86 (t=-2.77).
limits: Quasi-experimental: matched, not randomised. Tutor trained on the same test station used in the VTT. Tutored group got about 20 h of practice; controls did normal duty.
agent_relevance: Practice on a library of simulated faults plus coaching can lift novices to expert-level scores in about 20 h. Our agent could treat a stored set of solved faults as the practice set.

source: Gott, Kane, Lesgold (1995) Sherlock 2 effect sizes
finding: Effect sizes of Sherlock 2 on all posttests were large, well above the typical curriculum effect.
numbers: Table 9: VTT3 1.27 SD, VTT4 1.17 SD, NIT .87 SD, Frankenstation VTT .96 SD, Frankenstation NIT .76 SD. Report compares to 0.3 sigma for average new science and math curricula (Bloom, 1984).
limits: Control SDs are large (VTT SD 37 vs 5 for tutored), so effect sizes rest on a very uneven spread. Table text is OCR-garbled in the source copy; row order checked against means and SDs.
agent_relevance: Sets the benchmark size for what a good simulator-plus-coach can do.

source: Gott, Kane, Lesgold (1995) Frankenstation transfer test
finding: Transfer to a computer-controlled test station the airmen had never seen. Tutored novices still beat controls, so strategy and system knowledge transferred, not just procedures.
numbers: Frankenstation VTT: control 55 (n=21), tutored 82 (n=17), masters 91 (n=12); t=-2.93, p=.006. NIT: 72 vs 80 vs 88 (t=-2.34, p=.025). Fault solved in time: controls 63.6%, tutored 70.6%, masters 83.3%.
limits: Small cells; the solution-rate gap (70.6 vs 63.6) is small and no test is given in the text I read. Transfer is to a related electronics domain, not another trade.
agent_relevance: Cases teach transfer only if they carry strategy and system model, not procedure steps.

source: Gott, Kane, Lesgold (1995) behaviour differences in Frankenstation protocols
finding: Untutored airmen swapped parts without testing and used self-tests wastefully. Tutored airmen looked like masters.
numbers: Of 16 control self-test uses, 11 were inefficient (ran from the start until a fail). Experimentals 14 uses, 2 inefficient; masters 12 uses, 4 inefficient. Logical-sequence violations: controls 21 vs masters 9 (tutored count unreadable in the OCR copy).
limits: Counts are small and from verbal protocols coded by the authors. Some table cells are garbled.
agent_relevance: Tutor effect shows up as fewer premature swaps and better use of tools. A measurable behaviour for our agent: test before swap.

source: Lesgold, Lajoie, Bunzo, Eggan (1988) Sherlock: a coached practice environment for an electronics troubleshooting job
finding: Founding design paper. Sherlock gives the same ordered series of problems to everyone and individualises only the specificity of hints. The expert solution is kept as an abstracted problem space that drives hints and after-action review.
numbers: 34 problems, about 35 min each, about 20 h total; average student sees about 45 hints. Expert solved the sample problem in 7 steps; one trainee took 14, another 20. Reports Air Force evaluation: 20-25 h on Sherlock equals troubleshooting of colleagues with 4 more years on the job.
limits: The 1988 paper itself says comparative experiments had not been done: 'What is not yet evident is whether this approach matters.' The 4-year claim is cited to an in-press Nichols et al. report that I did not open.
agent_relevance: Design rule: fixed case sequence plus graded hints, with an expert path as reference. Maps onto a case library with an expert trace per case.

source: Lesgold et al. (1988) why a simulator is needed: rare faults
finding: Problem that motivates a simulator or case library: the hard skill is rarely practised on the job.
numbers: Routine work is about 95% of the time; test-station failure about once a month; first-term airmen (under 4 years) get few chances to learn repair.
limits: Author claims, not a measured dataset.
agent_relevance: Same logic as a case memory: it supplies rare cases that the agent has not met itself.

source: Katz & Lesgold (1992) Use of fuzzy modeling techniques in a coached practice environment (Sherlock II)
finding: Student model for Sherlock II uses fuzzy variables (probability distributions over skill levels) updated from coded performance (Good, OK, Bad), initialised at equal 20% over five levels.
numbers: Restates Sherlock I result: 20-25 h on system = proficiency of technicians with 4 years on the job (Nichols et al., in press). Each node of the goal tree hand-coded with needed knowledge components.
limits: Student model is expert-rule based; authors note an open fuzzy vs Bayesian debate. No new outcome data in this paper.
agent_relevance: A cheap way to track which kinds of faults an agent handles badly and choose cases to show.

source: Katz, Hall, Lesgold (1997) Cognitive task analysis and intelligent computer-based training: Sherlock, Hydrive, Eaglekeeper
finding: A tutor built from PARI task analysis (Precursor, Action, Result, Interpretation) works. A tutor for the same domain built without it showed no learning effect.
numbers: Sherlock: 18 tutored, 23 untutored, 13 masters; about 20 h over 3 weeks; VTT3 t[39]=-4.04, VTT4 t[39]=-3.72, both p<.001; Frankenstation t[36]=-2.93. Hydrive pre-post t[19]=4.14, p<.001; F-15 Pneudraulics tutor (single-expert input) and control showed no significant gain.
limits: Conference slides and transcript; Hydrive means only in a chart. Confounded: the two hydraulics tutors differ in content focus and in design process.
agent_relevance: What the cases teach matters more than having them. Case entries should tag strategy and reasons, not only steps.

source: Katz, Hall, Lesgold (1997) Hydrive effect by problem type
finding: Hydrive helped most where novices had to build their own strategy, and not where fault isolation guides were available.
numbers: Problem A (no guide): large Hydrive effect. Problem B (guide available): no group had an advantage. Task analysis found experts and novices equal in procedural skill but different in strategic knowledge.
limits: Exact means not readable in the text copy. Two problems only.
agent_relevance: Case libraries pay off on open diagnosis; when a procedure exists, retrieval adds little.

source: Katz, Hall, Lesgold (1997) three-knowledge model of troubleshooting
finding: Skill has three layers: procedural (easy, observable), system knowledge (learned by acting on equipment), strategic knowledge (what to do and when; develops last, after years).
numbers: Model drives content of Sherlock and Hydrive; Sherlock expert model has steps Investigate UUT, Investigate TP, Investigate TS.
limits: Descriptive model, not fitted to data in this document.
agent_relevance: Supports putting strategy-level hints into the case store.

source: Wikipedia: Case-based reasoning (history and 4-step cycle)
finding: CBR began with Schank and students at Yale in the early 1980s (Kolodner's CYRUS, Lebowitz's IPP). The cycle is retrieve, reuse, revise, retain (Aamodt and Plaza 1994). Early deployed systems: Lockheed CLAVIER, Compaq SMART.
numbers: International CBR conference since 1995. The article gives no performance numbers.
limits: Encyclopedia source, secondary. I did not open Aamodt and Plaza or Kolodner.
agent_relevance: The 4R cycle is the formal skeleton for a case-memory step in the scaffold.

source: Wikipedia: Intelligent tutoring system (effect sizes)
finding: Summaries of ITS meta-research: VanLehn (2011) found step-based ITS not different from expert human tutors; Kulik and Fletcher (2015) median 0.66 SD over conventional teaching. SHERLOCK listed as the F-15 troubleshooting tutor.
numbers: Median +0.66 SD (Kulik and Fletcher); about 200 development hours per hour of instruction (one cited estimate).
limits: Secondary summary; primary meta-analyses not opened. Development cost is a boundary.
agent_relevance: Sherlock's 0.8-1.3 SD is above the ITS median; build cost argues for reusing logged cases instead of hand-built tutors.

source: Tawfik & Jonassen (2013) The effects of successful versus failure-based cases on argumentation while solving decision-making problems (ERIC EJ1003059)
finding: Failure-case library beat success-case library on counterarguments and holistic argument scores, on both the library task and a no-library transfer task a week later.
numbers: N=36 undergraduate sales-management students, two conditions (success vs failure library); week 1 hiring decision, week 2 new similar case without library.
limits: Abstract only: no means or effect sizes. Small N. Ill-structured business decision, not fault diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Store failures as well as wins; failed attempts may carry more transferable content.

source: Tawfik, Kim, Hogan, Msilu (2019) How success versus failure cases support knowledge construction in collaborative problem-solving (EJ1225289)
finding: Failure-case group did better on conceptual-space understanding, knowledge-construction convergence and interaction; no difference on problem-space understanding.
numbers: Two conditions; no N or statistics in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Online collaborative setting.
agent_relevance: Second line of evidence for failure cases (failure-driven memory).

source: Tawfik (2017) Do cases teach themselves? Comparison of case library prompts (EJ1147638)
finding: A prompt to compare cases for reuse did worse than no prompt or a prompt to understand one case.
numbers: Three conditions: no prompt, 'retain' prompt, 'retrieval/reuse' prompt. No-prompt and retain beat retrieval/reuse on counterclaims and the holistic transfer score. N not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Argumentation task.
agent_relevance: Telling the learner to hunt for similarities can hurt; a boundary for forced analogy steps in the scaffold.

source: Tawfik, Kim, Kim (2020) Effects of case library recommendation system on problem solving and knowledge structure development (EJ1256252)
finding: Both static and recommended case libraries beat problem-based learning alone on initial arguments; the recommender was better on rebuttals.
numbers: Three conditions: PBL only, PBL + static library, PBL + recommendation library. N not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Retrieval quality (recommendation) added value on top of simply having cases.

source: Park, Park, Jung, Kim (2020) Promoting case indexing in case library learning (EJ1267204)
finding: Prompts that make learners index cases (by explanation or by difference) raised self-explanation and rebuttal quality.
numbers: N=105 students, three conditions: explanation-based prompt, difference-based prompt, none. Both prompt groups beat control on rebuttals; arguments still relied mostly on domain knowledge.
limits: Abstract only; career-course students, ill-structured problem.
agent_relevance: Indexing a case by what mattered in it is trainable; suggests the agent should write an index line when storing a case.

source: Tawfik et al. (2019) How novices use expert case libraries for problem solving (EJ1206656)
finding: Think-aloud shows five steps: index generation, prioritisation, alignment with prior knowledge, abstraction, reuse. Alignment and reuse were hardest.
numbers: N=5 junior marketing students.
limits: Tiny qualitative sample.
agent_relevance: Where a novice (or a weak model) fails in CBR: adapting a retrieved case, not finding it.

source: Hseih, Smith, Stephanou (2004) Use explicit hints in storytelling to help students solve ill-defined problems (ED485034)
finding: Describes a Jonassen-line story library of about 110 food-product stories and asks whether surface indices or deep indices (goal, plan, result, lesson) help. Cites Hernandez-Serrano (2001): a story library changed students' decisions, but students struggled to link stories to target problems.
numbers: About 110 stories; no outcome data in this record.
limits: Design proposal, no results.
agent_relevance: Indexing by deep features is the open question; same issue for retrieval keys in our case memory.

source: Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs (2025)
finding: LLM agent with an episodic case bank of (state, plan, success) records, retrieved by similarity or a learned Q-function, no weight updates. Case memory added gain on top of planning and tools.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3, test 79.40%. DeepResearcher avg F1/PM: offline executor 48.8/62.8; without case memory 59.9/72.2; full 66.6/80.4. SimpleQA 81.0/89.7 to 84.7/95.0. HLE 22.2/17.4 to 26.7/24.4. Out-of-distribution gains 4.7 to 9.6 points.
limits: GPT-4.1 planner and o3/o4-mini executors; authors note contamination. Case bank saturated after about 3k training items.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a case bank helps a scaffolded agent beyond planning.

source: Memento: how many cases to retrieve
finding: Best number of retrieved cases was 4; more did not help and could hurt, unlike few-shot prompting.
numbers: K in 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 on DeepResearcher: peak F1 64.5, PM 78.5 at K=4, then plateau or slight decline.
limits: One dataset.
agent_relevance: Retrieve a few cases, not many.

source: Memento: tools can hurt, case memory is additive
finding: Live tools alone lowered the DeepResearcher score (online executor 30.8/60.7 vs offline 48.8/62.8, -18.0 F1). Case memory gave steady additive gains over planning.
numbers: CBR gains over planning only: HLE +4.5 F1/+7.0 PM, SimpleQA +3.7/+5.3, DeepResearcher +6.7/+8.2.
limits: Authors suggest contamination explains the offline advantage.
agent_relevance: Gain from cases is modest but consistent; do not expect it to replace planning.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025, v2 2026) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Memory of distilled reasoning strategies from successes and failures (LLM-judged), not raw trajectories. Beats no-memory, Synapse and AWM.
numbers: WebArena overall success (684 tasks): Gemini-2.5-flash 40.5 none, 42.1 Synapse, 44.1 AWM, 48.8 ReasoningBank, 51.8 with MaTTS. Gemini-2.5-pro 46.7 / 53.9 / 56.3 (none / RB / MaTTS). Claude-3.7 41.7 / 46.3 / 48.8. Gains +8.3, +7.2, +4.6; steps down up to 16%.
limits: Judge was only 72.7% accurate against ground truth in the analysis, yet results were stable for 70-90% accuracy. Multi subset tiny (29 tasks).
agent_relevance: A case store of strategy lessons, not transcripts, is the better design.

source: ReasoningBank: value of failure cases
finding: Adding failed trajectories helped ReasoningBank but hurt or barely moved success-only memories.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: Synapse 40.6 to 41.7 with failures; AWM 44.4 to 42.2; ReasoningBank 46.5 to 49.7.
limits: One subset, one backbone.
agent_relevance: Echoes Tawfik and Jonassen (2013): failure cases only help if the store abstracts a lesson from them.

source: ReasoningBank: memory-aware test-time scaling (MaTTS)
finding: More parallel or sequential attempts help more when paired with memory; without memory the scaling gains were small and unstable.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: parallel k=1 49.7 to k=5 55.1; sequential 49.7 to 54.5. No-memory scaling fluctuated 39.0-42.2 (parallel) and 37.4-40.6 (sequential).
limits: Single subset.
agent_relevance: Several attempts plus a case store compound; fits our best-of-N plus scaffold arms.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Agent stores trajectories and extracts natural-language insights from success/failure pairs; at test time it retrieves similar trajectories and uses insights. Both parts matter.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% / 31%, ALFWorld 50% / 55%, WebShop 37% / 38%. Matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% vs 39% at round 3). ALFWorld with Reflexion rounds: retrieve-only 40.3 to 54.4; ExpeL 54.5 to 60.4; ExpeL with insights 59.0 to 64.2.
limits: Insights built from reflections hurt (hallucinated); learned insights beat hand-crafted ones. Four-fold validation on small task sets.
agent_relevance: Two memory types are complementary: case recall for action-heavy tasks, abstract insights for reasoning-heavy tasks.

source: ExpeL transfer HotpotQA to FEVER
finding: Insights learned on one task type transferred to another.
numbers: FEVER success: ReAct baseline 58, ExpeL transfer without task demos 63, intermediate 65, best 70 (column labels garbled in text extraction).
limits: Same API and Wikipedia domain; short transfer distance.
agent_relevance: Abstracted insights travel better than raw cases.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Induces reusable workflows from past successes and supplies them to the agent; works online without labels.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4) overall success 35.5 vs BrowserGym 23.5: +12.0 points, +51.1% relative; beats human-written workflows (SteP 32.0). Mind2Web cross-task +24.6% relative step success; out-of-distribution gains 8.9 to 14.0 points.
limits: Success-only memory; ReasoningBank later shows it degrades when failures are added (44.4 to 42.2). Table text partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Reusable routines work when tasks repeat templates; weaker evidence for novel faults.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Verbal self-reflections kept in an episodic buffer across trials improve later attempts; baseline for within-task case memory.
numbers: Absolute gains of 22% on ALFWorld in 12 steps, 20% on HotpotQA, 11% on HumanEval (91% pass@1 vs GPT-4 80%).
limits: Needs a reliable feedback signal; ALFWorld baseline hallucination plateaued near 22% with no recovery.
agent_relevance: Case memory without a trustworthy outcome signal can store wrong lessons.

source: Guo et al. (2024) DS-Agent: automated data science by empowering LLMs with case-based reasoning
finding: Full retrieve-reuse-revise-retain loop over Kaggle expert cases. Adjusting the retrieved case with execution feedback beats plain RAG.
numbers: Development: 100% success with GPT-4 on 12 tasks. Deployment one-pass rate 85% (GPT-3.5) and 99% (GPT-4) over 18 tasks vs best baseline 56% and 60%. Mixtral 6% to 31%. Ablation average best rank: full 2.08, without ReviseRank 2.58, without CBR 3.41. Cost $1.60 and $0.13 per run (GPT-4).
limits: Kaggle tasks with executable feedback, not diagnosis. Authors' own task set.
agent_relevance: Case revision from error feedback is worth building into the loop.

source: Guo et al. (2025) Optimizing CBR system for functional test script generation (Huawei, KDD 2025)
finding: Industrial CBR+LLM system; finetuned retriever and reuse step improved script quality and cut repetitive generation. Retaining new cases helped online.
numbers: Online test on about 6,000 samples: retain step gave FF1 gain of 2.75% (DCN) and 10.08% (SP); repetitive generation reduced by 2.47% and 2.41%.
limits: Proprietary data, two product units. Numbers read from partly garbled figure text.
agent_relevance: Shows retention of new cases pays in a deployed setting.
